objectives: Describe indirect rule in the British Cameroons
Describe the French system in Cameroun
Describe economic and social changes under both
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify: nature of indirect rule in the Southern and Northern Cameroons, French policy of assimilation vs association, the dates of completion of the Douala–Yaoundé railway (1920s) and of the CDC (1946), and use of forced labour.

Draft for teacher review: only well-established facts are used and the tone is neutral; every date and name must be verified against the official History syllabus and standard references before release.

blocks.md: The British ruled their Cameroons as part of Nigeria. They used **indirect rule**: they governed through **traditional rulers** and **native authorities**, who collected taxes, kept order and ran local courts under British officers. This was cheaper for Britain and kept many local customs. In the north and in the Grassfields, existing chiefs were used; in places without strong chiefs, new 'warrant chiefs' or councils were created.

blocks.caption: British and French administration
blocks.alt: Two columns comparing British and French systems.

blocks.title: French rule
blocks.md: The French used a more **direct** system, often called **assimilation** in principle: French officers governed districts with chiefs as lower agents, the **French language and culture** were taught in schools, and many Africans had to give **forced labour** and pay taxes. French Cameroun had its own administration under a High Commissioner, with a capital at Yaoundé.

blocks.title: Comparison
blocks.md:
- **British**: indirect rule, English, links with Nigeria, local chiefs kept authority.
- **French**: direct rule, French language, strong control by French officials.
- **Both**: collected taxes, built roads, required labour, promoted export crops and missions ran many schools.

**Economy and society.** Under both powers farmers produced **cash crops** (cocoa, coffee, bananas, palm oil), and roads and railways were built (the Douala–Yaoundé railway was completed in the French zone in the 1920s). After 1946 the former German plantations in the British zone were run by the **Cameroons Development Corporation (CDC)**. Mission and government **schools** and **clinics** expanded slowly; many children still had no access to school.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- British indirect rule did not mean the British had no power: it worked through chiefs but British officers had the final say.
- The French system was not the same in theory and in practice; it varied with place and period.
- Do not call a whole system 'good' or 'bad': compare its effects on different groups of people.

blocks.title: Example 1: indirect rule
blocks.statement: Why did the British use indirect rule?
steps: They had few officials and little money.
Using chiefs saved cost and kept order.
So it was cheap and practical.
blocks.answer: It was cheap and used existing leaders.

blocks.title: Example 2: language
blocks.statement: Name one effect of the different languages used by Britain and France.
steps: Schools taught in English or French.
Later each part used one of the two languages.
blocks.answer: Cameroon later had both English and French.
